warmup.q: You time 100 million calls of Math.sqrt(x) in a loop with System.nanoTime() and throw each result away. After a few rounds the loop reports 0.0000 ns per call. What is the best explanation?
options: Your CPU computes square roots in well under a nanosecond
The JIT saw that the results were never used and removed the work from the loop
System.nanoTime() is too coarse to measure such short calls
The JVM cached the result of the first call
warmup.why: No CPU does a square root in 0.0000 ns. Once C2 compiled the loop, it proved that nothing used the result of Math.sqrt(x) and deleted the call: dead-code elimination. nanoTime() resolution is fine for a 100-million-iteration loop, and the JVM has no result cache for Math.sqrt.

sections.h: A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer, not your code
sections.html:
Here is the benchmark almost everyone writes first:

Java
long t0 = System.nanoTime();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) {
    Math.sqrt(x);                      // result discarded
}
long t1 = System.nanoTime();
System.out.printf("%.4f ns/op%n", (t1 - t0) / 1e8);
Kotlin
val t0 = System.nanoTime()
for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) {
    sqrt(x)                            // result discarded
}
val t1 = System.nanoTime()
println("%.4f ns/op".format((t1 - t0) / 1e8))

It printed 0.0301, then 0.1299, then 0.0000 for every later round. A second loop that adds each result to a sum and prints the sum settled at about 1.9 ns per call. The JIT measured nothing in the first loop because, once C2 had compiled it, there was nothing left to measure. That is dead-code elimination: a computation whose result nobody uses can go.

Dead code is one of several ways a hand-made loop lies:

  • If the input is a constant, C2 can compute the answer at compile time, and you end up timing the load of one number. That's constant folding.
  • The first rounds run in the interpreter and in OSR code, as lesson 1 showed, and a benchmark that is one long loop in main keeps measuring OSR code.
  • The JIT unrolls loops and hoists work out of them. JMH's own sample on loops reports the measured cost of an addition falling "up to the point we do each addition with 1/20 ns, well beyond what hardware can actually do".

A wrong benchmark can also print a believable number, which is worse. On JDK 21, the same discarded loop with Math.log instead of Math.sqrt was not eliminated: it reported 7 to 9 ns per call, drifting upward from round to round. It looks plausible and still measures an accident of how C2 compiles Math.log. Whether the JIT can remove a call depends on what it can prove, and you can't see that from the outside.

try.title: Watch the work disappear
steps: Read NanoLoop. Predict both columns for round 1 and round 5.
Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin.
Change the discarded loop to Math.log(x) in either version and run it again.

code.title: NanoLoop.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l03; /** * The benchmark everyone writes first: a loop timed with System.nanoTime(). * Round by round it measures the same thing, twice: once with the result thrown away, * once with the result added to a sum that gets printed. */ public class NanoLoop { public static void main(String[] args) { double x = 2.0; for (int round = 1; round <= 5; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { Math.sqrt(x); // result discarded } long t1 = System.nanoTime(); double sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { sum += Math.sqrt(x + i); // result used } long t2 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)%n", round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum); } } }

alt.title: NanoLoop.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l03 import kotlin.math.sqrt // Kotlin twin of NanoLoop.java: the same naive nanoTime benchmark, with the result // thrown away and with the result used. fun main() { val x = 2.0 for (round in 1..5) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sqrt(x) // result discarded } val t1 = System.nanoTime() var sum = 0.0 for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sum += sqrt(x + i) // result used } val t2 = System.nanoTime() println("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)" .format(round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum)) } }

try.expect: The discarded column starts near 0.03 ns and becomes 0.0000 by round 3; the used column stays near 2 ns. Kotlin does the same. With Math.log, the discarded loop typically reports several nanoseconds per call instead of zero: on JDK 21 x86_64 C2 doesn't remove that call. Neither loop tells you the real cost of the method.

sections.h: JMH builds the measuring loop for you
sections.html:
JMH is the OpenJDK project's microbenchmark harness: the code that calls your method, times it and reports the result. Version 1.37, from August 2023, is still the latest release. You write a method annotated @Benchmark. JMH's annotation processor generates the measuring loop around it at compile time, written to defeat the tricks above, and a runner executes it in fresh JVMs.

A complete benchmark:

Java
@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)          // 5 x 1 s, results thrown away
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)     // 5 x 1 s, results kept
@Fork(2)                                   // two fresh JVMs
public class FeeBench {
    long amountCents = 123_456;            // input: a non-final field of the state object

    @Benchmark
    public long fee() {
        return FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents);   // returned: JMH consumes it
    }
}
Kotlin
@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Fork(2)
open class FeeBench {                      // JMH's generated code extends it, so it can't be final
    var amountCents = 123_456L             // var: an input nobody can predict

    @Benchmark
    fun fee(): Long = FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents)
}

The Kotlin class has to be open because JMH's generated classes extend it, and the build needs a plugin such as kotlinx-benchmark to generate the JMH code for Kotlin classes. This course keeps its benchmarks in Java.

What each piece does:

  • @State(Scope.Thread): one instance per benchmark thread. Its fields are your inputs.
  • @Setup: prepares state outside the measured time. Level.Trial, the default, runs it once per fork.
  • @Warmup and @Measurement: iterations and their length. Warm-up results are thrown away.
  • @Fork: how many fresh JVMs to run in. A new JVM has a clean profile, so one benchmark can't skew the next. @Fork(0) runs inside the JVM that launched it, which brings back every problem of the hand-made loop.
  • @BenchmarkMode: Throughput (the default, operations per time), AverageTime, SampleTime or SingleShotTime.
  • @Param: runs the benchmark once per value, as lesson 2's MegamorphicBench did with types.

The JMH 1.37 defaults are 5 forks, each with 5 warm-up and 5 measurement iterations of 10 seconds: more than eight minutes per benchmark method. That's on purpose. The demos in this track use 100 to 300 ms iterations so they finish quickly. That's fine for seeing a trap and too short for deciding anything.

You can run benchmarks from a main method with JMH's Runner and OptionsBuilder, as the demos do, or from a JMH uber-jar with command-line flags such as -f 2 -wi 5 -i 5 -prof gc.

try.title: Five ways to measure one square root
steps: Read TrapsBench. Predict which of the five benchmarks will score about the same as baseline.
Run it (under 10 seconds). Then run the Kotlin twin, which runs two of the five with JMH's full output so you can see the warm-up and measurement iterations go by.
Change double x = 2.0; to final double x = 2.0; and run the Java version again. Which benchmark changes?

code.title: TrapsBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.infra.Blackhole; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The same Math.sqrt measured five ways. The iterations are far shorter than JMH's defaults, so treat the numbers as rough. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class TrapsBench { double x = 2.0; // input from a non-final @State field static final double CONSTANT = 2.0; // input the JIT knows at compile time @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // the harness on its own @Benchmark public void sqrtDiscarded() { Math.sqrt(x); } // result thrown away @Benchmark public double sqrtReturned() { return Math.sqrt(x); } // JMH consumes the return value @Benchmark public void sqrtBlackhole(Blackhole bh) { bh.consume(Math.sqrt(x)); } @Benchmark public double sqrtOfConstant() { return Math.sqrt(CONSTANT); } // folded before it runs public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench.class.getName()) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10s %10s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var s = r.getPrimaryResult(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10.3f %10.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), s.getScore(), s.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: TrapsBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l03 // JMH benchmarks must be Java classes in this lab (the annotation processor runs on Java only). // This Kotlin twin runs the same Java benchmark through JMH's Runner API, but with JMH's // normal output, so you can see every warm-up and measurement iteration as it happens. import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode fun main() { val options = OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench::class.java.name + ".sqrt(Discarded|Returned)") // a regex: two of the five .verbosity(VerboseMode.NORMAL) .build() Runner(options).run() }

try.expect: sqrtDiscarded and sqrtOfConstant land on top of baseline, around 0.3 to 0.5 ns on the course VM. sqrtReturned and sqrtBlackhole are around 2 ns. With final double x = 2.0, javac copies 2.0 into every method, so sqrtReturned drops to the baseline as well. The Kotlin twin's log shows # Blackhole mode: compiler (auto-detected ...) and ends with JMH's "REMEMBER: The numbers below are just data" warning.

sections.h: Consume every result and read inputs from non-final fields
sections.html:
Two rules fix most broken benchmarks.

First, every result must reach JMH. The simplest way is to return it: JMH consumes return values. When there are two results, either combine them or pass each one to a Blackhole:

Java
@Benchmark
public void feeAndTax(Blackhole bh) {
    bh.consume(FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents));
    bh.consume(FeeMath.taxCents(amountCents));
}
Kotlin
@Benchmark
fun feeAndTax(bh: Blackhole) {
    bh.consume(FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents))
    bh.consume(FeeMath.taxCents(amountCents))
}

JMH's sample on Blackholes also says: if you have one result, return it, and "Do not make your benchmark code less readable with explicit Blackholes!" On JDK 17 and later JMH detects compiler blackholes, where the JIT itself treats consume as "used, and nothing else". The log says so in its header, and JMH warns that results from different Blackhole modes aren't comparable.

Second, inputs must come from non-final instance fields of the @State object. A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac copies the value into your method. javap on the lab's broken benchmark shows it:

public long fee();
   0: ldc2_w  #7      // long 123456l   <- the field is gone, the number is baked in
   3: invokestatic    FeeMath.feeCents:(J)J
   6: lreturn

From there C2 can fold the whole fee calculation into one number. JMH's constant-folding sample puts it bluntly: "IDEs will say 'Look, this field could be final'. Don't. Trust. Them." A static final input has the same problem, which is what sqrtOfConstant shows.

You can check both rules against a baseline. An empty @Benchmark method measures the harness alone (about 0.4 ns on the course VM). A benchmark that scores like the baseline is measuring nothing, whatever its name says. In a longer run on the same VM (2 forks of 5 one-second iterations), the empty baseline scored 0.365 ns/op, the discarded square root 1.09 and the constant one 0.545, while the returned square root and the Blackhole version took 3 to 6 ns. Short, noisy runs give different absolute numbers. Which benchmarks sit on the baseline stays the same.

Check yourself: a benchmark returns amount.multiply(RATE), where RATE is a static final BigDecimal and amount is a non-final @State field. Can C2 fold the whole result into a constant? (No. RATE is known, but amount can change between calls, so the multiplication has to run.)

sections.h: Measure allocation with -prof gc, because it doesn't wobble
sections.html:
Time is the noisiest thing you can measure. On a shared VM, the error bar on a short JMH run is often bigger than the score. Allocation is different: for the same code and input, a method allocates the same number of bytes every time. JMH's GC profiler (-prof gc, or addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) in code) reports it as gc.alloc.rate.norm, in bytes per operation.

MoneyBench sums 2.9% fees over 100 card payments, once with BigDecimal and once with long cents. One run on the course VM:

Benchmark            ns/op      error           B/op    error
feeBigDecimal       3551.2     7675.7      15200.082    0.200
feeLongCents         106.2      271.4          0.002    0.006

The time error is more than twice the score. The allocation is exact: 15,200 bytes per call, 152 bytes per line, every time. BigDecimal is right for money, and every multiply, setScale and add returns a new object. The long version allocates nothing. A separate, longer run got the same 15,200 B/op, and with 10,000 lines it was 1,520,003 B/op: allocation grows exactly with the number of line items.

That makes B/op the number to put in CI. A test can't assert "under 2 µs" without failing on a busy build agent, but it can assert "under 300 bytes per call", and lesson 7's lab does exactly that. Keep time measurements for quiet, dedicated machines, with several forks.

JMH has more profilers. -lprof lists the ones your machine supports. -prof stack samples thread stacks: on the BigDecimal benchmark it put 48.4% of samples in BigDecimal.<init>. The perf family (perfnorm, perfasm) needs Linux perf and shows hardware counters and the generated assembly. Every JMH run ends with a reminder worth reading once: "The numbers below are just data. To gain reusable insights, you need to follow up on why the numbers are the way they are."

try.title: Count the bytes
steps: Predict the B/op of each benchmark in MoneyBench, roughly.
Run it (about 7 seconds). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes.
Run the Kotlin twin. It writes the same two calculations in Kotlin (with * and += on BigDecimal) and counts bytes with the JVM's per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH.

code.title: MoneyBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Fees for 100 card payments: BigDecimal against long cents, with JMH's GC profiler on. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class MoneyBench { BigDecimal[] amounts; long[] cents; @Setup public void setup() { // built once per fork, outside the measurement amounts = new BigDecimal[100]; cents = new long[100]; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { cents[i] = 1_999 + i; amounts[i] = BigDecimal.valueOf(cents[i], 2); } } @Benchmark public BigDecimal feeBigDecimal() { // correct for money, and every operation allocates BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (BigDecimal a : amounts) { // a new rate object per line, as plenty of real fee code does total = total.add(a.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.029")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)); } return total; } @Benchmark public long feeLongCents() { // 2.9% in integer cents, rounded half up long total = 0; for (long c : cents) total += (c * 29 + 500) / 1000; return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(MoneyBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) // the same as -prof gc on the command line .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-14s %12s %10s %14s %8s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-14s %12.1f %10.1f %14.3f %8.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore(), bytes.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: MoneyBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l03 // MoneyBench.java measures with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This Kotlin twin runs // the same two fee calculations written in Kotlin and reads the JVM's per-thread allocation // counter around 100,000 calls: the same bytes-per-call idea as JMH's gc.alloc.rate.norm. // Allocation is steady enough to count this way. Time is not (remember NanoLoop). import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode private val amounts = Array(100) { BigDecimal.valueOf(1_999L + it, 2) } private val cents = LongArray(100) { 1_999L + it } fun feeBigDecimal(): BigDecimal { var total = BigDecimal.ZERO for (a in amounts) { // a new rate object per line; the operators call multiply and add total += (a * BigDecimal("0.029")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) } return total } fun feeLongCents(): Long { var total = 0L for (c in cents) total += (c * 29 + 500) / 1000 // 2.9% in integer cents, rounded half up return total } private val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var lastDecimal: BigDecimal? = null // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore private var lastCents = 0L private inline fun bytesPerCall(calls: Int, block: () -> Unit): Double { repeat(50_000) { block() } // warm up first, so C2 code is measured val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(calls) { block() } return (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before).toDouble() / calls } fun main() { val big = bytesPerCall(100_000) { lastDecimal = feeBigDecimal() } val small = bytesPerCall(100_000) { lastCents += feeLongCents() } println("feeBigDecimal: %10.3f B/op".format(big)) println("feeLongCents: %10.3f B/op".format(small)) println("(results: $lastDecimal, $lastCents)") }

try.expect: feeBigDecimal allocates about 15,200 bytes per call with an error under 1 byte, while its time error is huge on a busy machine. feeLongCents allocates 0. The Kotlin twin prints exactly 15200.000 and 0.000 B/op: Kotlin's BigDecimal operators call the same methods and allocate the same objects.

analogy: Benchmarking with a nanoTime loop is like timing a cashier by asking them to ring up the same item a million times while you watch. After the third time they stop scanning and type the total from memory, so you measure their memory. JMH is the mystery shopper: different baskets they can't predict (non-final inputs), every receipt checked (consumed results), a few practice rounds first (warm-up) and different shops on different days (forks). The analogy breaks because a cashier who stops scanning knows they're cutting corners. The JIT isn't cheating. Deleting unused work is its job, and your benchmark gave it permission.
world: Before you swap Jackson for another JSON library in the payment API, or BigDecimal for long cents in the ledger, someone will write a quick test with System.nanoTime() and paste a number in the pull request. Ask for a JMH benchmark instead, kept in the repository: @State with realistic payloads read from fields, results returned, -prof gc on, several forks. Put the B/op number in the PR description, since it will mean the same thing on your laptop and in CI. Treat the ns/op number as a rough guide unless it came from a quiet machine. For a Quarkus service, benchmark the plain Java code (the mapper, the fee rule, the validator), not the HTTP endpoint, which is load testing and a different tool.
mistake:
The most common mistake is a JMH benchmark that looks right and still measures nothing: a void method that discards its result, or an input in a final field with a constant initializer. Both compile, run and print a confident number, usually close to the baseline. The JIT removed or folded the work. The fix is mechanical. Return the result, or consume it in a Blackhole. Read inputs from non-final @State fields. Then add an empty baseline() benchmark and check that your real ones score clearly above it.

Java
private final long amountCents = 123_456;          // javac copies 123456 into fee()
@Benchmark public void fee() { FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents); }   // and the result is dropped
Kotlin
const val AMOUNT_CENTS = 123_456L                  // kotlinc copies it too
@Benchmark fun fee() { FeeMath.feeCents(AMOUNT_CENTS) }            // and the result is dropped

compare.title: Constants that get baked into the bytecode

java.title: Java
java.html: class Inputs { private final long amount = 123_456; // constant initializer: javac copies the value private final long fromCtor; // assigned in the constructor: a real field read long plain = 123_456; // what a benchmark input should be static final long RATE_BPS = 290; // copied by javac, and known to the JIT Inputs(long v) { fromCtor = v; } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: const val RATE_BPS = 290L // copied by kotlinc; RATE_BPS * 2 even becomes 580 open class Inputs(val fromCtor: Long) { // a real field read val amount = 123_456L // NOT copied: kotlinc reads the field var plain = 123_456L // what a benchmark input should be }

compare.note: Java copies any final field with a constant initializer into the code that uses it, instance fields included. Kotlin copies only const val. A Kotlin val amount = 123_456L compiles to getfield, as javap shows, so it isn't folded by kotlinc. Use var in a Kotlin benchmark anyway, because it says "input" to the next reader. Kotlin also folds arithmetic on constants at compile time: RATE_BPS * 2 compiled to ldc2_w 580. In either language, a benchmark that reads only constants measures the JIT's arithmetic, not yours.

worked.title: Turn a nanoTime test into a benchmark you can trust

steps.say: A pull request claims the new fee rule is "3x faster", based on this test. Spot the problems before reading on.
steps.code: @Test void newRuleIsFaster() { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) NewFeeRule.fee(12_345); // constant input, result dropped long newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) OldFeeRule.fee(12_345); long oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs); }

alt.html: @Test fun `new rule is faster`() { var t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { NewFeeRule.fee(12_345) } // constant input, result dropped val newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { OldFeeRule.fee(12_345) } val oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs) }

steps.say: Four problems: the results are dropped (dead code), the input is a constant (folding), the first loop warms up the JVM and the second inherits a warm JVM and a mixed profile, and a timing assertion in a unit test fails on a busy CI agent. Move the comparison to JMH, with the input in a non-final field.
steps.code: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) public class FeeRuleBench { long amountCents = 12_345; // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark public long oldRule() { return OldFeeRule.fee(amountCents); } // 2. returned @Benchmark public long newRule() { return NewFeeRule.fee(amountCents); } @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // 3. the floor to compare with }

alt.html: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) open class FeeRuleBench { var amountCents = 12_345L // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark fun oldRule(): Long = OldFeeRule.fee(amountCents) // 2. returned @Benchmark fun newRule(): Long = NewFeeRule.fee(amountCents) @Benchmark fun baseline() {} // 3. the floor to compare with }

steps.say: Add a @Param so the amount isn't one magic number, and turn on -prof gc so you get a stable second number. Self-check: why does @Param take strings? (Answer: JMH sets the field from text, one fork per value, so the values also show up in the results table.)
steps.code: @Param({"99", "12345", "9999999"}) long amountCents;

alt.html: @Param("99", "12345", "9999999") var amountCents = 0L

steps.say: Read the result with the error column, and check the baseline first. If newRule sits on the baseline, it measures nothing. If the error bars of the two rules overlap, "3x faster" isn't proven. And if newRule allocates 0 B/op where oldRule allocates 48, that's a result you can put in the PR whatever the timer says.
steps.code:
Benchmark                              (amountCents)  Mode  Cnt   Score   Error   Units
FeeRuleBench.newRule                           12345  avgt   15   ...     ...   ns/op
FeeRuleBench.newRule:gc.alloc.rate.norm        12345  avgt   15   ...     ...    B/op

lab.title: Fix three broken benchmarks
steps: Run the tests. Five of six fail; the sixth only checks that the classes are still JMH benchmarks. The tests never time anything: they call your benchmark methods and inspect them with reflection.
DeadFeeBench: make fee() hand its result to JMH.
ConstantFeeBench: make amountCents an input the compiler can't know. Keep the field name, because the test sets it to other values and expects fee() to follow.

ColdBatchBench: move building the batch into a @Setup method that runs once per fork, and keep only the summing in totalFees(). Then give it real warm-up (at least 3 iterations) and at least one fork.
Run the tests until all six pass. Optional: copy one fixed class into src/demo/.../l03, give it a main like TrapsBench's, and run it before and after your fix.
hints: For DeadFeeBench, changing void to long and adding return is the whole fix. A Blackhole parameter also passes, but one result reads better as a return value.
For ConstantFeeBench, look at javap -c -p on the compiled class before and after. Before: ldc2_w 123456. After: getfield amountCents.

In ColdBatchBench, add a long[] batch field and a @Setup(Level.Trial) public void buildBatch() method. Don't use Level.Invocation: it runs setup around every single call and distorts short benchmarks.
@Fork(0) runs the benchmark inside the JVM that launched it, with that JVM's profile and garbage. Use at least 1, ideally 2 or more.

drill.title: Write a correct benchmark from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a JMH benchmark that measures FeeMath.feeCents(amount) for a 1,000-payment batch built by Fixtures.batch(1000). Include the state, setup, warm-up, measurement, forks and mode. Then check it against the answer: is the batch built outside the measurement, is the result consumed, and are the inputs non-final fields?

answer.html: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) public class BatchFeeBench { int size = 1_000; long[] batch; // non-final input @Setup(Level.Trial) // once per fork, not measured public void build() { batch = Fixtures.batch(size); } @Benchmark public long totalFees() { long total = 0; for (long cents : batch) total += FeeMath.feeCents(cents); return total; // consumed by JMH } }

alt.html: @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) open class BatchFeeBench { var size = 1_000 lateinit var batch: LongArray // non-final input @Setup(Level.Trial) // once per fork, not measured fun build() { batch = Fixtures.batch(size) } @Benchmark fun totalFees(): Long { var total = 0L for (cents in batch) total += FeeMath.feeCents(cents) return total // consumed by JMH } }

recap: A hand-made nanoTime loop measures the optimizer: dead code is removed (0.0000 ns/op), constants are folded, the first rounds run cold, and loops get unrolled and hoisted.
JMH generates the measuring loop, runs warm-up iterations it throws away, then measurement iterations in fresh JVMs (@Fork), and reports a score with an error.
Return every result or consume it in a Blackhole, and read inputs from non-final @State fields. A final constant field is copied into your method by javac.
Compare against an empty baseline() benchmark: anything that scores like it is measuring nothing.
-prof gc gives gc.alloc.rate.norm in bytes per operation. It is steady enough to gate in CI; time is not.

explain.prompt: A teammate pastes "new mapper: 12 ns/op, old mapper: 40 ns/op" from a loop timed with System.nanoTime(). Explain, in your own words, why you don't trust it yet and what you'd ask for instead.
explain.answer: A hand-made loop measures whatever the JIT left behind. If the mapper's result isn't used, C2 can delete the work; if the input is a constant, it can fold it; the first loop runs partly in the interpreter while the second runs in a warmed-up JVM with a profile the first one shaped. So 12 versus 40 might measure dead code, warm-up order or OSR. I'd ask for a JMH benchmark with the payload in a non-final @State field, the mapped result returned, an empty baseline to compare with, a few forks so each run gets a fresh JVM, and -prof gc so we also get bytes per operation, which is stable enough to trust and to check in CI.

deeper.html:
Three more JMH features are worth knowing before you need them.

@State(Scope.Benchmark) shares one state object across all benchmark threads, and @Threads(4) or @Group runs several threads at once. That is how you measure contention, for example 4 threads incrementing one AtomicLong against a LongAdder. Lesson 4 talks about why those differ.

Mode.SampleTime records a distribution of individual call times and prints percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), which fits latency questions better than an average. Mode.SingleShotTime measures one call per iteration, which suits cold-start questions.

JMH's padding is automatic for @State objects: the JMH false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your state object can still share a cache line, which is lesson 4's topic.

If you want to see what C2 really did to a benchmark, -prof perfasm prints the hottest generated assembly next to the counters. It needs Linux perf and the hsdis disassembler. Without it, the cheap check is the one you already know: put an empty baseline next to every benchmark and be suspicious of anything that scores like it.
